solution.concept_anchor: Section 14 moratorium — inclusions and exclusions

statement_analysis.statement: The moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC prohibits the institution of any suit or proceeding against the corporate debtor in any court or tribunal during the CIRP period.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 14 expressly prohibits institution of suits and continuation of pending proceedings against the corporate debtor in any court, tribunal, or arbitration — this is a core moratorium protection.

statement_analysis.statement: The moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC extends to personal guarantors of the corporate debtor, protecting them from recovery proceedings during the CIRP period.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 14 moratorium applies to the corporate debtor only — it does not extend to personal guarantors, who remain exposed to recovery proceedings by lenders during the CIRP period.

statement_analysis.statement: During the moratorium period, the corporate debtor is prohibited from paying statutory dues such as GST and provident fund contributions, as these would constitute transfers of assets.
statement_analysis.reason: The moratorium prohibits transfer, encumbrance, or disposal of assets by the corporate debtor, but the corporate debtor is required to continue operational payments including statutory dues — regulatory compliance payments are not prohibited by Section 14.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the moratorium prevents 'all proceedings' may incorrectly assume it also covers guarantors, making Statement 2 appear correct when it is the incorrect one.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: prohibition of suits and proceedings against the corporate debtor is a core Section 14 protection — Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: moratorium does not shield personal guarantors — they face separate proceedings; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: statutory dues payment is not barred by the moratorium; only asset transfers/encumbrances are restricted — Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 2 and 3 are incorrect — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the scope-extension error. The Supreme Court has explicitly held (in Lalit Kumar Jain v. Union of India, 2021) that the Section 14 moratorium does not extend to personal guarantors — lenders can pursue guarantors even while the CIRP is ongoing. Many students assume the moratorium's broad language covers all persons associated with the corporate debtor, which is incorrect.
solution.final_explanation:
Section 14 of IBC imposes a moratorium on the corporate debtor immediately upon CIRP commencement — a critical protection to preserve the debtor as a going concern during resolution.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 14 prohibits institution and continuation of suits, proceedings, and arbitral proceedings against the corporate debtor — this is the core of the moratorium.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The moratorium protects the corporate debtor, not its personal guarantors. The Supreme Court in Lalit Kumar Jain (2021) confirmed that lenders retain the right to proceed against personal guarantors during CIRP.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The moratorium bars disposal, encumbrance, or transfer of assets — it does not prohibit the corporate debtor from meeting its regular operational obligations including statutory payments (GST, PF, ESI). Suspending statutory payments would itself violate other laws.

Statements 2 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (d).

Value Addition:
• Section 14 also prohibits recovery of any property by an owner or lessor where the property is occupied or in the possession of the corporate debtor.
• The moratorium ceases on approval of a resolution plan or commencement of liquidation.
• Supply of essential goods and services to the corporate debtor cannot be terminated during the moratorium.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 29A — promoter eligibility when NPA account resolved before CIRP bid
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Section 29A bars promoters of NPA accounts assume the bar is absolute and select option (c), not knowing the ArcelorMittal case clarification that paying off the NPA before bid submission removes the disqualification.
elimination_logic: Identify the applicable law: Section 29A of IBC governs resolution applicant eligibility — promoters of accounts classified as NPA for 1 year or more are prima facie disqualified.
Identify the key fact in the scenario: the promoter's related company has a separate NPA account — not the company under CIRP itself.

Recall the ArcelorMittal judgment: the Supreme Court held that if the disqualifying NPA account is paid off/regularised before the resolution plan is submitted, the disqualification under Section 29A is cured.
Eliminate option (c): the bar is not unconditional and absolute — payment of the NPA before submission cures the disqualification.
Eliminate option (a): mere disclosure does not cure the disqualification; actual payment of the NPA account does.
Eliminate option (d): Section 29A applies to corporate insolvency proceedings including CIRP — it does not exempt promoters based on the sector.
Option (b) correctly applies the ArcelorMittal principle — select (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the common assumption that Section 29A's disqualification is absolute and permanent. The ArcelorMittal judgment introduced the nuance that a promoter disqualified due to a related NPA account can cure the disqualification by paying off that NPA account in full before submitting the resolution plan. Students who know the general disqualification but not this specific judicial gloss will select option (c).
solution.final_explanation:
Section 29A creates a threshold-based ineligibility framework to prevent defaulting promoters from regaining control of stressed assets at discounted prices through the resolution process.

Scenario analysis: The promoter seeking to submit a resolution plan has a separate corporate entity with an NPA classified for over 12 months. Under Section 29A(c), such a promoter is prima facie disqualified.

However, the ArcelorMittal and Essar Steel (2019) judgment established a critical qualification: if the resolution applicant makes payment of the outstanding amount of the NPA account (the separate entity's account) before submitting the resolution plan, the disqualification is cured. This prevents a windfall but allows genuine turnaround investors to participate.

Why each option fails:
• Option (a): Mere disclosure does not cure Section 29A disqualification — active payment is required.
• Option (b): Correct — if the promoter pays off the related NPA account before submitting the plan, the disqualification under Section 29A is removed.
• Option (c): The bar is not unconditional; the ArcelorMittal ruling provides the cure mechanism.
• Option (d): Section 29A applies across sectors — no manufacturing exemption exists.

Value Addition:
• Section 29A(j) defines 'connected person' broadly to prevent indirect circumvention via shell entities.
• The 'lookback period' for NPA classification under Section 29A was debated extensively in ArcelorMittal — the court held it applies at the time of plan submission.
• Section 240A of IBC exempts MSMEs from certain Section 29A restrictions to allow promoter-led resolution.

solution.concept_anchor: Recovery mechanisms and their statutory thresholds
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) incorrectly pairs the SARFAESI loan threshold with the DRT minimum claim, which are the two most easily confused threshold figures in the NPA resolution ecosystem.
elimination_logic: Match A (90-day overdue norm): this is the NPA classification threshold under RBI's IRAC norms — matches Item 3.
Match B (₹20 lakh minimum claim): DRTs exercise jurisdiction only over claims above ₹20 lakh under RDDBFI Act — matches Item 2.
Match C (₹1 crore minimum default): CIRP under IBC can be triggered for defaults of ₹1 crore or more (post-2020) — matches Item 4.
Match D (loan above ₹1 lakh, security interest required): SARFAESI threshold conditions — matches Item 1.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap operates between the SARFAESI threshold (₹1 lakh) and the DRT threshold (₹20 lakh). These are two different thresholds in the same recovery ecosystem and are frequently conflated. Option (a) swaps them — presenting ₹20 lakh as the SARFAESI threshold and ₹1 lakh as the DRT minimum. Students who have not retained both figures precisely will select the swapped version.
solution.final_explanation:
Each NPA resolution mechanism operates above a specific threshold — these figures are frequently tested in UPSC examinations.

Correct pairings:
• A–3: The 90-day overdue norm is RBI's universal NPA classification trigger under IRAC norms. An account overdue for more than 90 days becomes an NPA.
• B–2: DRT jurisdiction under RDDBFI Act, 1993 is exercisable only for claims of ₹20 lakh or above — claims below this go to civil courts.
• C–4: The minimum default threshold for triggering CIRP under IBC was raised to ₹1 crore in March 2020 from the original ₹1 lakh.
• D–1: SARFAESI applies to loans above ₹1 lakh where the outstanding NPA exceeds 20% of principal+interest and where a security interest has been created.

Trap pairings to avoid: The ₹1 lakh and ₹20 lakh figures are easily swapped — SARFAESI's ₹1 lakh threshold (loan minimum) is distinct from DRT's ₹20 lakh (claim minimum).

Value Addition:
• SARFAESI's ₹1 lakh is the floor for the underlying loan, not the NPA amount — separate from the 20% NPA threshold condition.
• The ₹1 crore CIRP threshold was introduced specifically to reduce NCLT's caseload and protect MSMEs during COVID-19.
• For PIRP (MSME pre-pack), the maximum default threshold is ₹1 crore — it coincides with CIRP's minimum.

solution.concept_anchor: PIRP vs. CIRP — debtor-in-possession, Swiss challenge, timeline

statement_analysis.statement: In a Pre-packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PIRP), the existing management of the MSME retains control of business operations throughout the resolution period, unlike in CIRP where the Resolution Professional takes over management.
statement_analysis.reason: PIRP is a debtor-in-possession model — existing promoters/management remain in place. This is the fundamental structural difference from CIRP's creditor-in-control model.

statement_analysis.statement: PIRP is available to all corporate debtors regardless of their size, provided the default amount does not exceed ₹1 crore.
statement_analysis.reason: PIRP is available only to MSMEs (as defined under the MSMED Act, 2006) — it is not available to all corporate debtors. The ₹1 crore default ceiling is correct, but the class eligibility is restricted to MSMEs.

statement_analysis.statement: Under PIRP, if the Committee of Creditors rejects the base resolution plan submitted by the debtor, a Swiss challenge process is initiated, allowing third-party applicants to submit competing plans.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the distinctive Swiss challenge mechanism of PIRP — if the CoC finds the debtor's base plan unsatisfactory, it can invite third-party bids, which must match or better the terms of the rejected base plan.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as true may include Statement 2 if they recall only the ₹1 crore ceiling without noticing the MSME-only eligibility restriction.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: debtor-in-possession is the defining characteristic of PIRP — Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: PIRP eligibility is restricted to MSMEs — it is not available to 'all corporate debtors' — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Swiss challenge upon CoC rejection of base plan is an accurate description of PIRP procedure — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 contains a scope-extension error. The ₹1 crore default ceiling is correctly recalled but the candidate who stops there misses the class restriction: PIRP is available only to MSMEs, not to all corporate debtors. A student who partially reads the provision and focuses on the monetary threshold will affirm Statement 2, leading them to select option (d) instead of option (c).
solution.final_explanation:
PIRP was introduced to provide a faster, less disruptive insolvency pathway for MSMEs that preserves existing management relationships and reduces resolution costs.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The debtor-in-possession model is PIRP's most significant structural departure from CIRP. Existing management continues to run the business while the resolution plan is negotiated — critical for MSMEs where business value is tied to the promoter's relationships and expertise.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: PIRP eligibility is restricted to MSMEs as defined under the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (MSMED) Act, 2006. The ₹1 crore maximum default ceiling is correct, but the 'all corporate debtors' characterisation is wrong — large corporates are ineligible for PIRP.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Swiss challenge mechanism ensures that if the CoC rejects the debtor's base plan, the process does not collapse — third parties can bid, but must match or improve on the base plan terms, protecting the debtor's first-mover advantage.

Value Addition:
• PIRP's 120-day timeline is approximately one-third of CIRP's 330-day outer limit.
• PIRP was operationalised through the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2021 and related Rules.
• Section 240A of IBC provides MSMEs special treatment, including exemption from certain Section 29A disqualifications.

solution.concept_anchor: Indradhanush framework — seven elements
solution.strong_distractor: b — 'De-stressing PSBs' (resolving legacy NPAs) sounds like a structural reform distinct from capitalisation, but it is actually one of the seven Indradhanush pillars — making it a genuine Indradhanush element that students might mistakenly exclude.
elimination_logic: Recall the seven pillars of Indradhanush: Appointments (Bank Board Bureau), Bank Board Bureau formalisation, Capitalisation, De-stressing, Empowerment, Accountability, and Gyan Sangam.

Option (a): Establishing the Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd with sovereign guarantee — this describes the NARCL (2021 bad bank), not an Indradhanush element. NARCL was announced 6 years after Indradhanush.
Options (b), (c), (d): De-stressing, empowerment of PSB management, and Bank Board Bureau are all confirmed Indradhanush pillars.
The odd one out is option (a) — select (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges two distinct government initiatives separated by six years. Indradhanush (2015) is a 7-element reform package; NARCL/bad bank (2021) is a separate NPA resolution initiative. Students familiar with multiple government banking initiatives may conflate them, especially since both address PSB stress. The mention of 'sovereign guarantee' in option (a) is the giveaway — Indradhanush had no such ARC component.
solution.final_explanation:
Indradhanush (2015) was the government's comprehensive reform blueprint for public sector banks — named after the seven-colour rainbow symbolising its seven reform pillars.

• Option (a) — Odd one out: Establishing a government-guaranteed Asset Reconstruction Company for legacy NPAs was announced in Union Budget 2021-22 as NARCL — not part of Indradhanush (2015). This is the odd element.
• Option (b) — Part of Indradhanush: De-stressing PSBs by resolving legacy NPAs was the fourth Indradhanush pillar, focusing on reducing NPA accumulation through sector-specific remediation.
• Option (c) — Part of Indradhanush: Empowerment of PSB management — giving boards greater operational autonomy — was the fifth pillar.
• Option (d) — Part of Indradhanush: Bank Board Bureau (now Bank Investment Company) to professionalise PSB governance was the second pillar.

Value Addition:
• Gyan Sangam was an annual two-day banking conclave launched under Indradhanush — attended by PSB chiefs and senior government officials.
• The Appointments pillar of Indradhanush separated the Chairman and MD & CEO roles in PSBs.
• Indradhanush was the precursor to the larger recapitalisation announcements of ₹2.11 lakh crore in 2017.

solution.concept_anchor: Government dues rank below unsecured financial creditors in liquidation

statement_analysis.statement: Under Section 53 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, government dues (including tax arrears) rank below unsecured financial creditors in the priority order for distribution of liquidation proceeds.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 53 explicitly places government dues below unsecured financial creditors in the waterfall — a deliberate departure from earlier statutory regimes that gave government preferential status.

statement_analysis.statement: This ordering was introduced to ensure that the government, as a sovereign entity, does not bear any loss from corporate insolvency proceedings.
statement_analysis.reason: The ordering was NOT designed to protect the government from losses — in fact, by ranking government dues lower, the government bears greater risk of non-recovery. The rationale was to incentivise institutional creditors by assuring them of superior recovery priority, making insolvency resolution commercially viable for financial system participants.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know government dues rank below unsecured creditors (Statement 1 correct) may assume the stated rationale in Statement 2 is also the legislative intent, without critically examining whether sovereign protection is the actual purpose.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Section 53 liquidation waterfall is unambiguous — government dues rank below unsecured financial creditors; Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: the claim that this order protects the government from losses is factually inverted — ranking lower means the government bears more loss risk, not less. The actual purpose is to incentivise private creditors; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's reversed-causation trap is particularly effective because the causal explanation sounds superficially plausible — students may think a sovereign would only accept a lower ranking if it guaranteed them some protection. In reality, the government's lower ranking was a deliberate policy choice to make India's insolvency framework commercially attractive to institutional lenders and foreign capital, accepting greater government exposure to corporate losses in exchange for better-functioning credit markets.
solution.final_explanation:
The positioning of government dues in the IBC liquidation waterfall was among the most debated policy choices when the Code was designed.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Section 53 waterfall places government dues (taxes, statutory levies) below unsecured financial creditors. This means in liquidation, banks and bondholders receive proceeds before the government's tax claims are satisfied.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The rationale is the opposite of what is stated. By ranking below unsecured creditors, the government absorbs greater residual risk. The policy purpose was to attract institutional lending and investment into distressed assets by assuring financial creditors of priority recovery — a pro-market design choice. This contrasts with older statutes (like the Companies Act pre-IBC regime) where government dues had preferential status.

Value Addition:
• Under the pre-IBC Companies Act regime, the Crown (government) debts had preferential status over most private creditors — IBC reversed this priority.
• The Supreme Court in Moser Baer (2019) affirmed that IBC's Section 53 waterfall overrides other statutes granting government dues priority.
• Workmen dues for 24 months rank above secured creditors — a social protection carve-out within an otherwise market-oriented waterfall.

solution.concept_anchor: Security Receipts — QIB investors in ARC structure
solution.strong_distractor: a — 'Retail investors through stock exchange platforms' sounds plausible in a post-digitisation era where many financial instruments are retailised, leading students unfamiliar with ARC regulations to select this option.
elimination_logic: Recall that ARCs raise funds from investors by issuing Security Receipts — these are restricted instruments not available to retail investors.
SRs are issued to Qualified Institutional Buyers (QIBs) — a regulatory category covering banks, insurance companies, mutual funds, and pension funds.
Eliminate option (a): retail investors through stock exchanges cannot subscribe to Security Receipts.
Eliminate option (b): the government does not subscribe to SRs issued by conventional ARCs — government backing applies only to NARCL's SRs through guarantee.
Eliminate option (d): NBFCs as a general category are not the exclusive or primary SR investors — QIBs is the precise and correct category.
Select option (c): Qualified Institutional Buyers.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap replaces 'Qualified Institutional Buyers' with plausible-sounding alternatives. The QIB category is a specific regulatory classification under SEBI and RBI frameworks — it includes banks, insurance companies, mutual funds, FPIs, and similar institutional investors. Students who know SRs are investable instruments but have not retained the QIB-specific restriction will select option (a) or (d).
solution.final_explanation:
Security Receipts (SRs) are instruments issued by Asset Reconstruction Companies to raise funds for purchasing stressed assets from banks.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: SRs are not listed or traded on stock exchanges for retail investors. They are restricted instruments distributed privately to qualified institutional participants.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The central government does not subscribe to SRs issued by conventional ARCs. Government backing (guarantee) applies specifically to NARCL's SR issuance under the bad bank model — conventional ARCs have no such sovereign backing.
• Option (c) — Correct: Under SARFAESI and RBI regulations, Security Receipts can only be issued to Qualified Institutional Buyers (QIBs) — a defined category including scheduled commercial banks, insurance companies, mutual funds, provident funds, and registered FPIs.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: While some NBFCs may qualify as QIBs individually, 'all registered NBFCs' is an overbroad and inaccurate characterisation — the investor class is QIBs, not NBFCs generically.

Value Addition:
• ARCs typically use a 15:85 structure — 15% cash payment and 85% in SRs — when acquiring NPAs from banks.
• SRs are redeemable over time as the ARC resolves the underlying assets.
• RBI has been pushing for a higher cash component in ARC acquisitions to ensure genuine price discovery and reduce contingent liabilities on banks holding SRs.

solution.concept_anchor: CoC voting thresholds — 66% resolution, 75% liquidation

statement_analysis.statement: A resolution plan under IBC requires approval from CoC members holding at least 66% of the voting share of financial creditors.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 30(4) of IBC prescribes a 66% voting share threshold for CoC approval of a resolution plan — reduced from the original 75% by the 2019 amendment.

statement_analysis.statement: A decision to liquidate the corporate debtor requires approval by CoC members holding at least 75% of the voting share.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 33 of IBC requires 75% of CoC voting share to pass a resolution for liquidation — this asymmetry (66% for resolution, 75% for liquidation) is a deliberate design to favour resolution over liquidation.

statement_analysis.statement: Under PIRP, the debtor's base resolution plan is approved if supported by CoC members holding 66% of the voting share, the same as in CIRP.
statement_analysis.reason: Under PIRP, the CoC evaluates the base plan but the voting mechanics differ — specifically, if the CoC rejects the base plan with 66% votes, it triggers the Swiss challenge, not a direct liquidation. The threshold framework is not identical to CIRP for all decisions.

statement_analysis.statement: The Resolution Professional in a CIRP can cast a tie-breaking vote in the CoC if the voting is equally split between financial creditors.
statement_analysis.reason: The Resolution Professional facilitates and records CoC decisions but has no voting rights — the RP cannot cast a tie-breaking or any other vote in the CoC.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 2 as correct may include Statement 3 if they assume PIRP voting thresholds are identical to CIRP thresholds, making 'Only three' seem correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: 66% for resolution plan approval — correct (post-2019 amendment).
Statement 2: 75% for liquidation — correct (asymmetric design).
Statement 3: PIRP voting framework is not identical to CIRP in all respects — the statement oversimplifies; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statement 4: RP has no voting rights in CoC — Statement 4 is incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 2 are correct — select option (b): Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap in Statement 1 is subtle: the original IBC threshold for resolution plan approval was 75%, which was reduced to 66% by the 2019 amendment. Students who studied IBC before 2019 or from outdated sources may recall 75% as the resolution threshold and mark Statement 1 incorrect while marking Statement 2 incorrect too — creating maximum confusion. The 66%/75% asymmetry (resolution vs. liquidation) is the most commonly confused CoC threshold pairing.
solution.final_explanation:
CoC voting thresholds are among the most precisely tested IBC facts in competitive examinations.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 30(4) requires 66% CoC voting share for resolution plan approval. The original 75% threshold was reduced to 66% by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2019.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Section 33 requires 75% for a liquidation decision — the asymmetry is intentional. A lower bar for resolution (66%) and a higher bar for liquidation (75%) encourages creditors to prefer viable resolution over destructive liquidation.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: PIRP has a distinct procedural framework. While 66% is used for plan approval in PIRP as well, the consequences of rejection (Swiss challenge initiation) and the overall framework differ from CIRP. Claiming they are identical oversimplifies.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The Resolution Professional is a facilitator and process manager — they have no voting rights in the CoC. Voting is exercised only by financial creditor members.

Only two statements (1 and 2) are correct — answer is 'Only two.'

Value Addition:
• Before the 2019 amendment, resolution plan approval required 75% — the same as liquidation, creating perverse incentives.
• CoC voting share is proportional to the financial debt owed to each creditor, not equal per creditor.
• IRP (Interim Resolution Professional) manages the debtor until the RP is formally appointed by the CoC.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 35AA ultra vires ruling — specific government authorisation requirement
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know the Supreme Court struck down the February 2018 circular may assume the Reason must be wrong because 'Section 35AA grants RBI general powers' — confusing general regulatory powers with the specific case-by-case authorisation requirement.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The Supreme Court in April 2019 struck down RBI's February 2018 circular on resolution of stressed assets.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Section 35AA of the Banking Regulation Act requires the central government to specifically authorise RBI for each direction it issues to banks regarding insolvency of a specific borrower. The February 2018 circular issued blanket directions without such specific authorisation — making it ultra vires.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. The Supreme Court's holding was precisely that Section 35AA requires a specific government direction for each instance, and the blanket circular violated this — R is the direct and accurate causal explanation for A.
A correct + R correct + R explains A → select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in option (c) tempts students who know the circulars were struck down to assume the Reason must be wrong — perhaps because they vaguely recall RBI has broad regulatory powers. The key precision is that Section 35AA specifically requires case-by-case government authorisation for directions about specific borrower insolvency — and blanket circular directions across all borrowers simultaneously violated this requirement. Students who know the outcome but not the precise Section 35AA requirement will select (c).
solution.final_explanation:
The Supreme Court's April 2019 judgment in Dharani Sugars & Chemicals Ltd. v. Union of India was a landmark ruling that reshaped RBI's approach to stressed asset resolution.

Assertion (A) is correct: RBI's February 2018 circular, which mandated resolution plans within 180 days for accounts in default, was struck down by the Supreme Court in April 2019.

Reason (R) is correct and is the direct causal explanation: Section 35AA of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 empowers RBI to issue directions to banks but requires the central government to specifically authorise each such direction regarding insolvency of a specific borrower. The February 2018 circular was a generalised direction covering all large accounts simultaneously — without specific government authorisation for each account. The Supreme Court held this exceeded RBI's powers under Section 35AA, making the circular ultra vires.

R correctly explains A — both A and R are correct, and R is the accurate causal explanation.

Correct answer: (a)

Value Addition:
• Following the judgment, RBI issued a revised circular in June 2019 incorporating a 30-day review period and ICA-based resolution framework.
• Section 35AB (separate from 35AA) grants RBI general powers to issue guidelines on resolution of stressed assets — the February 2018 circular could not rely on 35AB either.
• The ruling did not question RBI's overall regulatory authority, only the procedural compliance with Section 35AA for directions relating to specific borrower insolvency.

solution.concept_anchor: Twin balance sheet — transmission to GDP and infrastructure concentration

statement_analysis.statement: The twin balance sheet problem in India refers to simultaneous stress on the asset quality of banks and the excessive leverage on the balance sheets of large corporate borrowers, particularly in infrastructure-linked sectors.
statement_analysis.reason: The Economic Survey's characterisation of the twin balance sheet problem precisely identifies these two co-existing stresses — bank NPAs and corporate over-leverage — concentrated in infrastructure, power, steel, and related sectors post-2008.

statement_analysis.statement: The primary transmission channel through which the twin balance sheet problem affected India's GDP growth was the contraction of private investment due to tightened credit availability from stress-impaired banks.
statement_analysis.reason: Stressed banks reduced new credit disbursement to preserve capital ratios, creating a credit crunch that depressed corporate investment and contributed to GDP deceleration — this is the standard transmission mechanism documented in Economic Surveys.

statement_analysis.statement: Recapitalisation bonds issued by the government address the 'Resolution' element of the 4R strategy, as they directly resolve the underlying NPA accounts on bank balance sheets.
statement_analysis.reason: Recap bonds address 'Recapitalisation' — the third R — by restoring bank capital buffers. They do not directly resolve the underlying NPA accounts; NPAs remain on bank books until resolved through SARFAESI, IBC, or other mechanisms.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know recapitalisation is part of the 4R strategy may incorrectly affirm Statement 3, confusing the capital restoration function of recap bonds with the resolution function of legal mechanisms.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: the twin balance sheet definition with infrastructure concentration is accurately stated — Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: credit crunch → investment contraction → GDP deceleration is the documented transmission mechanism — Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: recap bonds restore capital (Recapitalisation), not resolve NPAs (Resolution) — Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, Statement 3 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 employs a partial-truth strategy: recapitalisation bonds are correctly associated with the 4R framework, but incorrectly assigned to the 'Resolution' element rather than 'Recapitalisation.' A student who correctly recalls '4R' but has not retained which R corresponds to which instrument will affirm Statement 3. The distinction between Resolution (using IBC, ARCs) and Recapitalisation (using bonds, budget) is a frequently tested conceptual boundary.
solution.final_explanation:
The twin balance sheet problem shaped India's economic policy debates from 2015 to 2020 and generated the 4R strategic framework.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Twin balance sheet stress: (i) banks — rising NPAs impairing balance sheets; (ii) large corporates — excessive debt from the 2008–12 infrastructure investment boom unable to service obligations. Infrastructure, power, telecom, steel, and real estate were the most affected sectors.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The transmission channel ran from impaired banks → reduced credit disbursement → corporate investment contraction → GDP deceleration. This is documented in Economic Survey 2016-17 and subsequent annual reports.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Recapitalisation bonds address the third R (Recapitalisation) — they restore the capital base of banks so they can resume normal lending. The 'Resolution' element (second R) encompasses IBC proceedings, SARFAESI enforcement, ARC-based resolution, and one-time settlements — not capital infusion instruments.

Value Addition:
• India's gross NPA ratio peaked at approximately 11.2% in March 2018 before declining steadily.
• The Economic Survey 2016-17 introduced the term 'balance sheet syndrome with Indian characteristics.'
• Evergreening (rolling over bad loans as new credit) was a major pre-AQR practice that masked the true NPA level.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap exploits the IBBI-NCLT confusion. Students who associate IBBI with 'overseeing everything IBC' may assign CIRP admission powers to IBBI. In fact, IBBI is a regulatory body — it cannot admit or reject insolvency applications. NCLT has exclusive adjudicatory jurisdiction for corporate CIRP. The complaint against the RP is correctly within IBBI's quasi-judicial disciplinary mandate.
solution.final_explanation:
The IBC framework carefully separates adjudicatory and regulatory functions across different bodies.

Scenario analysis:
Event 1 — CIRP application admission: This is an adjudicatory act. NCLT is the designated adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency proceedings under IBC. NCLT benches examine CIRP applications and pass orders for admission or rejection. IBBI has no adjudicatory role in individual CIRP applications.

Event 2 — Complaint against Resolution Professional: This is a regulatory-disciplinary matter. IBBI oversees the conduct of Insolvency Professionals (IPs) and Insolvency Professional Agencies (IPAs). If an RP is accused of misconduct, IBBI has quasi-judicial powers to investigate, call for records, and impose penalties including deregistration.

Why each option fails:
• Option (a): RBI has no role in CIRP proceedings or RP disciplinary matters.
• Option (b): IBBI cannot admit CIRP applications — that is NCLT's exclusive jurisdiction.
• Option (c): NCLT adjudicates CIRP matters but has no mandate to investigate and penalise RPs as a class — that is IBBI's regulatory domain.
• Option (d): Correct division — NCLT for CIRP adjudication, IBBI for RP regulatory oversight.

Value Addition:
• NCLAT (National Company Law Appellate Tribunal) hears appeals against NCLT orders in IBC matters.
• IBBI can refer matters to NCLT for contempt if its investigation orders are not complied with.
• Insolvency Professional Agencies (IPAs) provide first-level oversight of IPs; IBBI is the apex regulator above IPAs.

A large steel manufacturer defaults on its loan repayments. A consortium of lenders files an application to initiate Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP). Separately, a creditor files a formal complaint that the Resolution Professional appointed in a related insolvency case has been colluding with the promoter and selectively withholding financial information from the Committee of Creditors.

Which of the following correctly identifies the authority competent to address each of the above situations?

(a) Reserve Bank of India — for both the CIRP initiation and the complaint against the Resolution Professional
(b) Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India — for both the CIRP initiation and the complaint against the Resolution Professional
(c) National Company Law Tribunal — for both the CIRP initiation and the complaint against the Resolution Professional
(d) National Company Law Tribunal — for CIRP initiation; Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India — for the complaint against the Resolution Professional
